A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same NuiScene work. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and can be matched despite reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original reconstruction and generation experiments, resource measurements, timing comparisons and generated-scene examples.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds reconstruction, scaling, sensitivity and multi-scene results in Appendix C.

M1.justification: Appendix C.3 introduces a decoder variant for 13-scene training: a channel projection and pixel-shuffle-like reshape expand features to 512 vectors, followed by three additional self-attention layers. This is a localized architectural extension; the original encoder, losses and conditional outpainting framework remain.

E1.justification: Both versions study outdoor-scene reconstruction and generation using NuiScene43. The new 13-scene experiment expands the training subset within this collection, but does not identify a distinct new domain, dataset or task; its scene and chunk counts are experimental-setting changes.

E2.justification: Triplane, RePaint and Trellis remain the comparison methods. Within the existing four-scene setting, v2 adds quantitative triplane comparisons in Tables 10–11, whereas v1 presents vector-set generations and a qualitative Trellis comparison.

E3.justification: v2 completes the 128-by-128 triplane experiment using four L40S GPUs instead of the unsuccessful two-GPU setting. New experiments vary batch sizes and inference resolutions, evaluate four-scene diffusion with 30k quad-chunks per distribution, and train on 280k chunks from 13 scenes. The original single-scene split and principal training settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix C adds substantial sensitivity and failure analyses: high-resolution triplane artifacts, larger-batch overfitting and height errors, inference resolutions of 13/25/50, and the decoder upsampling comparison for 13-scene training. These extend considerably beyond v1's resolution comparisons, RePaint analysis and qualitative examples.

E5.justification: Table 5 first specifies that generation times are averaged over five runs; v1 gives no repetition count. This establishes a reporting change, not an increase from a known earlier run count. Neither version reports timing dispersion or confidence intervals.

E6.justification: Tables 2–4 retain their numerical results, but Table 5 revises timings: explicit vector-set generation/decoding changes from 217.79/76.59 seconds to five-run averages of 215.92/87.76 seconds. New entries in Tables 7–11 report high-resolution, larger-batch and four-scene outcomes. The 128-by-128 triplane achieves predicted-height F-score 0.879 versus vecset's 0.864, while the new 13-scene decoder variant raises IoU from 0.968 to 0.983 within that experiment.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, normalization, losses and diffusion equations remain substantively unchanged. Algorithm 1 clarifies the denoising call, but no new formal assumptions, derivations, propositions or proofs are introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract and four introduction contributions retain the same claims: efficient vector-set representation, explicit outpainting, cross-scene blending and NuiScene43 curation. The shorter conclusion preserves this scope; the new appendix experiments primarily supply additional support.

C2.justification: Appendix C adds substantive qualifications concerning floating artifacts, larger-batch overfitting, height-prediction failures and decoder capacity. It also explains why marching-cubes thresholds and differing chunk distributions limit CD/F-score comparisons across settings, favoring IoU for those comparisons. These materially deepen the interpretation beyond v1's mainly dataset-size, controllability and global-context limitations.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies 50 DDPM denoising steps, 12-view retrieval embeddings, camera field-of-view and clipping settings, and TRELLIS-image-large without decimation. It adds dataset-visualization and sampling-configuration links and documents the new decoder variant. These disclosures do not by themselves establish changes to previously performed experiments.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to Objaverse-XL, DreamFusion and pixel-shuffle super-resolution. Its limitations discussion expands positioning relative to 2D-prior methods and directly supervised 3D generation, while the main related-work coverage and novelty framing remain.

P1.justification: v2 tightens prose, shortens the conclusion, separates Limitations into its own section and brings a scene-texturing summary into the main text. The supplement is reorganized from S1–S3 into A–C, while the overall narrative and much of the wording remain.

P2.justification: The supplementary presentation expands substantially with Tables 7–11, height-error and resolution comparisons, decoder-comparison panels, and aerial/street-level views of 13-scene generations. Existing meshes are widely re-rendered in blue, Figure 6's detail annotations are revised, and earlier galleries are reduced or replaced. Main-text tables are also relocated.

improvement.justification: v1 supports multi-scene generation mainly through qualitative examples and leaves its highest-resolution triplane baseline unevaluated because of memory limits. v2 adds four-scene quantitative comparisons, 13-scene validation and completed high-resolution and larger-batch experiments, alongside specific failure analyses and metric caveats. These substantially strengthen empirical scrutiny and reproducibility; the benefit is better-supported, more qualified evidence rather than uniformly higher performance.
